title: Nobody at Atlassian has to come in. More of them do every year.
author: Brian Elliott
summary: Brian Elliott uses Atlassian as a counterexample to both return-to-office mandates and the push to abandon offices altogether. Although the company is distributed-first and requires no set number of days, office attendance rose 9% year over year. He draws on Atlassian's Alisa Yu, MillerKnoll's Ryan Anderson and Cloudflare's Caroline Quick to explain why: when AI makes execution cheap, coordination becomes the scarce resource, and offices become places for ideating, calibrating and recovering. He argues that leaders should aim for employees to "re-attach" to the office rather than "return" to it, using team-owned spaces, project rooms and purposeful gatherings. His practical advice for leaders is to treat AI transformation as emotional team work, measure earned rather than mandated attendance, build flexible spaces and write voice norms before buying pods.
points: Atlassian's rising attendance without any mandate shows that choice does not have to mean empty offices, and that earned attendance is a stronger signal than enforced attendance.
As AI makes execution cheap, the scarce resource shifts to coordination, so offices built for individual desk work and pre-booked meeting rooms are mismatched to what teams now need together.
Atlassian's ideate, calibrate and regulate framework gives leaders a concrete spec for space: low-surveillance room for ideas, fast decision rooms, and space to recover from AI-driven brain fry.
Reframing return to office as re-attachment draws on place attachment research and points to cheap tactics such as team neighborhoods, persistent project rooms and gatherings with a real reason.
Leaders should measure whether the trip was worth it rather than counting badge swipes, citing Atlassian data that intentional gatherings lift team engagement by 27%.
quotes: Nobody in that building had to be there, which should truly irritate the sh*t out of you if you’re currently arguing with your CEO about badge swipes.

Giving people choice over where they work changes the entire dynamic. When coming together is an act of agency rather than a policy requirement, a vibrant space and strong community become a true magnet. There’s no badge tracking required.
Alisa put the mechanism in one line: “When execution gets really cheap, coordination becomes the scarce resource.

Offices today are really built on yesterday’s model, assuming that the hardest part of knowledge work is execution. Most of them have a sea of individual desks, and they also have a lot of conference rooms, with an underlying assumption that meetings are pre-scheduled.
Nobody shares an uncertain idea (let alone internal heresy) in a room when there’s a blinking red light on the camera in front of them.
We shouldn’t talk in terms of return to office,” Ryan said. “It should be about re-attach to office, so that both places feel like it’s mine and it’s special to me, for different reasons.
Attendance you mandate and attendance you earn look identical on a report. The number worth watching isn’t how many people came in, it’s whether the trip was worth it and whether they’d come back.
AI transformation is emotional work; come together. If a group is talking about how to use AI, redesigning workflows and wrestling with the emotional issues around change, that’s jazz ensemble work.
